documents: Fahim, W.K. 2022. Saint Anthony Cave: Morphology, genesis, and age of one of the oldest religious shrines, Southern Galala Plateau, Eastern Desert, Egypt. Journal of Cave and Karst Studies 84(4): 105-118 (published PDF)

entry.evidence: Saint Anthony Cave had been described as a phreatic cave in previous research, but the cave lacked a detailed map and its speleogenesis was unclear.

sequences.source_document: Fahim 2022, Journal of Cave and Karst Studies 84(4): 105-118

steps.action: States the open problem: the cave was described as phreatic but had no detailed map, and its speleogenesis was unclear.
steps.quote: the cave lacked a detailed map and its speleogenesis was unclear

steps.action: Takes from the literature the rival origins of arid-zone dissolution caves (epigene carbonic acid versus hypogene mechanisms) and Halliday's phreatic, fossil-outflow interpretation of this cave.
steps.quote: Other caves have no apparent genetic relationship to surface recharge and have certain characteristics suggesting hypogenic speleogenesis.

steps.action: Uses the author's earlier simple map, which placed the cave's formation at or below the water table.
steps.quote: Fahim (2019) provided a simple map of the cave and confirmed that the cave had formed at or below the water table.

steps.action: Sets the aim: survey and map the cave, describe its morphology and speleothems, and use regional background to determine controls and speleogenetic phases.
steps.quote: [...] this work was to survey the cave and produce a detailed map and to describe the cave morphology in detail

steps.action: Describes the setting: scarp-face dissolution features, mineral-filled fractures, climate record, host lithology, and spring hydrochemistry (partly from cited data).
steps.quote: The scarp face has a corrosion surface with a variety of dissolution features

steps.action: Compares corrosion tables, flat-ceiling pendants and likely gypsum in the active spring caves below with features typical of sulfuric acid caves.
steps.quote: These features are common in sulfuric acid caves (e.g., Audra et al., 2009) and suggest that sulfuric acid may have been involved

steps.action: Assembles the published regional tectonic, volcanic, stratigraphic and uplift history of the Gulf of Suez Rift and Wadi Araba.
steps.quote: Omar et al. (1989) used apatite fission track analysis on the rocks of the western margin of the Gulf of Suez rift

steps.action: Surveys the cave with compass, clinometer, laser range finder and tape, processes the data in ArcGIS, identifies minerals by field HCl test, and reports the map and dimensions (22.13 m2, 17.10 m long, 5.33 m deep).
steps.quote: We surveyed the cave in detail on June 15 and August 3, 2021

steps.action: Compares the orientations of the passage and room fractures with the rift-parallel (clysmic) and transverse fault trends of the Gulf of Suez Rift.
steps.quote: The trend of the fracture of the cave passage is called “clysmic” or “rift parallel.”

steps.action: Describes meso- and micromorphology: the overlying branch, the sealed floor fissure, the cupola-like feature, bell holes, dissolution pockets and hollows.
steps.quote: The most significant feature of Saint Anthony Cave is an upward branch of the upper-level entrance passage.

steps.action: Correlates one paleowater level inside the cave with a notch in the cliff face outside.
steps.quote: There is a definite correlation between the elevation of one paleowater level inside the cave and a notch in the cliff face outside the cave.

steps.action: Measures paleowater levels relative to a datum and inventories speleothems inside and outside the cave (thick calcite layer, mammillary coatings, flowstone, spar, banded flowstone like alabaster).
steps.quote: In the entrance passage, 3 major paleowater levels are present at 2.10 m, 0.95 m, and 0.60 m above the datum.

steps.action: Compares the new observations with the prior phreatic interpretation and with settings known to favour hypogene speleogenesis.
steps.quote: Our new results support that origin with new observations of paleowater-level dissolution features and at least four phases of cave development.

steps.action: Rejects an epigene, surface-recharge or floodwater origin because sinkholes, sinking streams and shafts are absent, catchment drainage runs opposite to the cave gradient, and floodwater features are lacking; backflooding is allowed only as a later process.
steps.quote: There is no strong speleogenetic relationship between the cave and overlying or adjacent surface features.

steps.action: Infers from feature relationships a feeder fissure, a former cave extent beyond the threshold, the thick calcite layer as an earliest-phase relic, and inundation after subaerial deposition.
steps.quote: Paleowater level features superimposed on the subaerial speleothems suggest inundation following subaerial deposition.

steps.action: Compares the external flowstone with Egyptian calcite-alabaster and its cited hydrothermal temperatures, notes scalenohedral crystals and convection features, and reclassifies some springs as slightly thermal by Schoeller's threshold, concluding thermal paleowater was likely present.
steps.quote: The thermal paleowater was present in the past and likely contributed to the development of the cave.

steps.action: Keeps sulfuric acid dissolution as an open rival: suggestive features are present, but no gypsum has been found.
steps.quote: While the remaining evidence is inconclusive, dissolution by sulfuric acid cannot be ruled out.

steps.action: Brackets the timing of the phreatic phase between Chattian rift onset and Burdigalian uplift, using burial depth, rift-related fracture trends, cited erosion and sand-isolith data, and sea-level curves.
steps.quote: the phreatic phase of the cave is no younger than Burdigalian or probably no older than the beginning of the opening

steps.action: Proposes that speleogenesis began at rift onset, driven by volcanism-related CO2/H2S and thermal water rising along deep-rooted faults, possibly through several mechanisms.
steps.quote: We propose that the speleogenesis initiated with the onset of the rifting.

steps.action: Builds the four-phase sequence (phreatic dissolution and precipitation; late Miocene subaerial speleothems; post-Miocene submergence and dissolution; later speleothem deposition), matched to cited climate and sea-level history.
steps.quote: The main phases of the development of the Saint Anthony Cave.

steps.action: Retains the four-phase, hypogene-influenced, uplifted phreatic origin as the conclusion.
steps.quote: This study identified four phases of cave development caused by different processes at different times

tree.answer: A relict, small, fracture-controlled cave of unclear origin
Morphology yes (surveyed); genesis and age no, known only from traces
Map the cave and reconstruct its speleogenetic controls and phases
Epigene surface recharge versus hypogene deep fluids; within hypogene, CO2/H2S, thermal water, mixing, sulfuric acid
Qualitative: surface connection and floodwater features versus feeders and paleowater and condensation features
Found, not set; field traces and regional geological history
No deliberate variation or independent check reported
Four-phase, hypogene-influenced phreatic origin kept as best explanation; sulfuric acid left open
Reviewers acknowledged; no review file supplied

end.claim: Saint Anthony Cave is a multi-phased uplifted cave formed mainly under phreatic conditions with deep, likely thermal fluids from late Oligocene rifting, followed by late Miocene speleothem growth, post-Miocene submergence and dissolution, and later speleothem deposition.

decisive_move.sentence: Bracketing the phreatic phase between Chattian rift onset and Burdigalian uplift, from burial depth, fracture trends and cited regional erosion and sea-level records, is what gives the phases their ages; without it the claim would be a description of morphology only.

gates.evidence: The fieldwork was a mapping and description survey that no hypothesis directed (p. 107). The epigene rival was checked against surface features it would predict and rejected (p. 113), but the phase ages rest on regional analogy with no direct dating, so the headline claim faced no test it could clearly fail. Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: ArcGIS 10.3 for cave survey processing and mapping
Laser range finder, compass and clinometer for cave survey and paleowater-level heights
Monks' information and monastery records (spring discharge since the 1st century AD, sealed floor fissure)
Field hydrochloric acid test for mineral identification

novelty_claims.quote: New, detailed mapping using ArcGIS shows the cave has an area of 22.13 m2 with a length and depth of 17.10 m and 5.33 m, [...]
[...] the cave is a multi-phased uplifted cave formed primarily under phreatic conditions, with later modification by rising water levels.
A detailed map has been created of Saint Anthony Cave.

limits: No speleothem or host-rock dating (U-Th, isotopes) was performed; all phase ages are inferred from cited regional tectonic, sea-level and climate histories, and the author defers isotopic work to future studies (p. 116). Minerals were identified only by field observation and HCl, so the claims about calcite and alabaster are unverified. The cave floor and lower walls are obscured by concrete and structures, and the floor fissure is known only from monks' testimony. The study covers a single cave with no independent replication. Sub-claims at weaker status: thermal water in the 3rd phase is likely, best_explanation at low confidence; sulfuric acid dissolution is unresolved, status none; the depositional phases of the mammillary coatings and the thin calcite layer are undetermined; the four-phase timing is a best_explanation resting on analogy. The map dimensions are direct observations. Inference: the acknowledgements say a reviewer read the manuscript more than once and a colleague corrected a misunderstanding of the geological structure, so the tectonic section was probably revised, but no review file was supplied and no review sequence is coded. The paper is single-authored but uses 'we'.

disagreements.target: Halliday (2000; 2001; 2003), phreatic interpretation of Saint Anthony Cave
disagreements.support: New mapping and paleowater-level features support the phreatic origin, but the paper adds deep hypogene fluids and four phases, with onset tied to Oligocene rifting.
disagreements.quote: This study complements previous work and interpretation of the speleogenesis of Saint Anthony Cave [...] .

disagreements.target: Khalil et al. (2021); Wannous et al. (2021), classification of the springs as cold
disagreements.support: Applying Schoeller's 4 °C threshold to Wannous et al.'s own temperature data, a few springs come out as slightly thermal.
disagreements.quote: Those latter few springs are considered slightly thermal or warm according to the 4 °C threshold of Schoeller (1962).

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Epigene surface recharge; floodwater cave; backflooding from Wadi Araba
alternatives_considered.reason: No sinkholes, sinking streams or shafts; catchment drains opposite to the cave gradient; floodwater features not distinct

alternatives_considered.chosen: Sulfuric acid dissolution kept as possible
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Ruling sulfuric acid in or out
alternatives_considered.reason: Suggestive features present but no secondary gypsum; evidence inconclusive
A normal fault above the entrance has a similar dip and strike

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Mammillary coatings formed early and were preserved, or formed in a later phase
Overlying section as a sub-horizontal passage or a modified chimney, from an early or a later phase
